title: The table matters
hook: the biggest portion may suit your stomach, but not the fellowship of the table (Enchiridion 36)
carry: for the sake of the fellowship

segments.voice: Yesterday: the side door, and the right thing done in plain view. Your line was without the side door. What did you do openly? Day three hundred seventy-one.

A platter comes around the table. Four pieces of chicken left, and one of them is clearly the biggest. Everyone sees it. Everyone pretends not to. There's a small, silent negotiation going on, and you may have been on both sides of it. Epictetus, of all people, uses this moment to teach a bit of logic. Section thirty-six starts like a textbook on reasoning and ends at a dinner party. Today, to close the week: the table matters.
screen: `FOUR PIECES LEFT. ONE IS BIGGEST.` → `A LOGIC LESSON AT DINNER.` → `THE TABLE MATTERS.`

segments.voice: First, the logic. Take two statements: it is day, it is night. Joined with or, it is day or it is night, they make a perfectly good statement. Joined with and, it is day and it is night, they make a false one. Same pieces. Different combination. The value depends on how they're joined. Second, the dinner. In the same way, Epictetus says, at a shared meal, taking the biggest portion may have value for your body taken alone. But joined to the table, to the company and the host, it loses that value. So the larger share is to be avoided, for the sake of the fellowship of the meal. Third, what to look at. When you eat with someone, he says, don't only weigh what the food on your plate is worth to your body. Keep in view the respect owed to your host. The meal is not just food. It's a relationship being kept, one plate at a time. Fourth, why a Stoic cares. Back in section fifteen, life was a banquet, and we learned to take a modest share when the dish reaches us. Today goes one step further. The smaller portion isn't only self-control. It's a way of honoring the people at the table. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: mostly quiet. Yes means yes. Ask, don't tell. He missed the rest. Wait. No need to hide. Every one of them, like today's, is about living well alongside other people.
screen: `DAY OR NIGHT: TRUE. DAY AND NIGHT: FALSE.` · `THE BIGGEST PORTION, JOINED TO THE TABLE.` · `KEEP THE HOST IN VIEW.` · `THE SMALLER PORTION HONORS THE TABLE.` · then, large: `THE TABLE MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Picture the next meal you'll share with someone, at home, at work, anywhere. See the table, the faces, the food going around. Now see yourself, quietly, taking the smaller portion, or letting someone else choose first. No announcement. Notice how it feels to put the table ahead of your plate for a moment. Then let the picture go, and just breathe. The bell holds the time.
Banquet. Life as a shared meal, Epictetus says elsewhere; the biggest portion may suit your body, but not the fellowship of the table. Today's word.
Your line: for the sake of the fellowship. At one shared meal today, take the smaller portion, or let someone else choose first. Day three hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism take the smaller share at shared meals and let others choose first, as a small way of honoring the company and the host.

original.note: Greek: a drinking party or banquet, where English symposium comes from; Epictetus' shared meal.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be greedy.
what it means: a thing good for you alone can be bad joined to others; the shared table changes its value.
what a scholar hears: Stoic logic, an or-statement versus an and-statement, applied to who takes the biggest portion at dinner.

notes: Enchiridion 36 paraphrased: 'it is day' and 'it is night' have value in a disjunctive proposition but none in a conjunctive; so at a banquet the larger share may be valuable for the body but should be avoided to keep the social character of the feast; keep the respect due to the host.
